problem: 'Latmos' is unexplained; most modern readers will not know it is the mountain of Greek legend, so Rochester's identification of the picture's setting is lost.
new_text: "Not completely: you've caught the shadow of your thought, but no more, probably. You lacked enough of the artist's skill and knowledge to give it full life. Yet the drawings are, for a schoolgirl, unusual. As for the ideas behind them—they are otherworldly. Those eyes in the Evening Star you must have seen in a dream. How did you make them look so clear yet not at all bright? The planet above dims their light. And what meaning lies in their solemn depth? And who taught you to paint wind? There's a fierce gale in that sky and on that hilltop. Where did you see Latmos, the mountain of the Greek legend? For that is Latmos. There—put the drawings away!"

problem: Phrenology reference ('mass of intellectual development', 'curve of benevolence' on the forehead) is opaque without knowing the period belief that skull shape revealed character; 14.27 only explains it afterwards.
new_text: He lifted the dark waves of hair that lay across his brow, revealing—by the phrenologists' reading of skulls—a solid enough mass of intellectual development, but a notable deficiency where the gentle curve of benevolence should have risen.

problem: '(said quietly!)' is confusing as an aside; the sense is that he lowers his voice so Mrs. Fairfax (one of the 'old women') won't hear.
new_text: "There again! Another jab of the penknife when she pretended to pat my head. And that is because I said I did not like the company of children and old women (not so loud!). No, young lady, I am not a general philanthropist; but I do have a conscience"—he pointed to the bumps on his skull said to indicate that quality, which were, fortunately for him, quite prominent, giving a marked breadth to the upper part of his head—"and besides, I once had a kind of rough tenderness of heart. When I was your age, I was a feeling sort of fellow, partial to the young, the unprotected, and the unlucky. But Fortune has knocked me around since then: she has even kneaded me with her knuckles, and now I flatter myself I am hard and tough as a rubber ball—with a crack or two still open, though, and one sensitive point in the middle. Yes—does that leave hope for me?"

problem: Untranslated French 'et j'y tiens' is not clear from context; a brief in-line gloss helps readers and listeners.
new_text: "Stubborn?" he said. "And irritated. Ah! That is consistent. I put my request in an absurd, almost rude form. Miss Eyre, I apologize. The fact is, once and for all, I don't wish to treat you as an inferior. That is"—he corrected himself—"I claim only the advantage that must come from twenty years' difference in age and a century's advance in experience. This is fair, et j'y tiens—I insist on it—as Adèle would say. And it is by virtue of this advantage, and this alone, that I ask you to be good enough to talk to me a little now and distract my thoughts, which are raw from dwelling on one point—festering like a rusty nail."

problem: 'My tenderest feelings are about to receive a shock—such is my feeling' repeats 'feeling' awkwardly and obscures that he is making a prediction (which the next sentence tests).
new_text: "Never mind—wait a moment. Adèle is not ready for bed yet. My position, Miss Eyre, with my back to the fire and my face to the room, gives me a good view. While talking to you, I have also been watching Adèle from time to time (I have my own reasons for finding her a curious study—reasons I may, indeed shall, share with you someday). She pulled from her box, about ten minutes ago, a little pink silk dress. Rapture lit her face as she unfolded it. Coquetry runs in her blood, blends with her mind, and seasons the marrow of her bones. 'Il faut que je l'essaie!' she cried, 'et à l'instant même!' and she rushed from the room. She is now with Sophie, being dressed up. In a few minutes she will come back, and I know what I shall see—a miniature of Céline Varens, as she used to appear on stage at the rise of—but never mind that. My tenderest feelings are about to receive a shock—or so I predict. Stay now and see whether it comes true."

problem: Over-long sentence with a garbled clause: 'when in an elegant closed carriage ... I recognized the carriage I had given Céline' (a carriage recognized inside a carriage). Split for listeners.
new_text: "I liked sweets too in those days, Miss Eyre, and I was crunching chocolate bonbons and smoking by turns, watching the carriages roll along the fashionable streets toward the nearby opera house. Then, clearly visible in the brilliant city night, came an elegant closed carriage drawn by a beautiful pair of English horses: I recognized it as the carriage I had given Céline. She was returning: of course my heart pounded against the iron railing I leaned on. The carriage stopped, as I expected, at the hotel door; my flame (the very word for an opera mistress) stepped out. Though wrapped in a cloak—an unnecessary covering on so warm a June evening—I knew her instantly by her little foot, visible beneath the hem of her dress as she hopped from the carriage step. Leaning over the balcony, I was about to murmur 'Mon ange'—in a tone, naturally, meant only for the ears of love—when a figure jumped from the carriage after her, also cloaked. But that was a spurred heel that rang on the pavement, and that was a hatted head that now passed under the arched entrance of the hotel.

problem: Dangling modifier: 'continuing his walk in silence, I ventured' grammatically makes Jane the one continuing his walk.
new_text: Adèle ran up to him with her shuttlecock. "Away!" he cried harshly. "Keep your distance, child; or go in to Sophie!" Then, as he continued his walk in silence, I ventured to bring him back to the point from which he had abruptly wandered—

problem: Paragraph repeats Rochester's question from 15.43 verbatim after Jane has already answered it (15.44), then 15.46 says he 'listened very seriously' — reads as a non-sequitur/duplication. Not in the known-caption list; likely an unlisted illustration-caption artifact. If it must stay for alignment, add it to the known-artifact list or blank it; do not leave it as a spoken line.

Rochester says 'I must visit the second floor', but the laugh's footsteps went to the 'third-floor staircase' (15.32) and 'ascending to the third floor' (15.44), and he then opens that staircase door (15.51). Readers will be confused about where he goes.
new_text: "Not at all. Just stay still. You have a shawl on. If you're not warm enough, take my cloak over there; wrap it around you and sit in the armchair. There—I will put it on for you. Now put your feet on the stool, to keep them out of the wet. I am going to leave you for a few minutes. I will take the candle. Stay where you are until I return. Be as still as a mouse. I must visit the third floor. Don't move, remember, or call anyone."

problem: 'sago' is unfamiliar to most modern readers; making it 'sago pudding' signals it is a dish she prepares.
